messages.content: What is the freezing point point of water at a pressure of 10 kPa?

function.name: thermodynamics_calculate_boiling_point
function.description: Calculate the boiling point of a given substance at a specific pressure. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

pressure.description: The pressure at which to calculate the boiling point. This is a float type value.

message.content:
**Answer**

At a pressure of **10 kPa** (≈ 0.1 atm) the freezing (melting) point of pure water is only **slightly above 0 °C** – roughly **+0.01 °C** (about 0.02 °F).  

---

### Why it’s a little above zero

Water’s solid–liquid equilibrium line (the melting curve) has a **negative slope** in the pressure–temperature phase diagram.  
That means:

* As pressure **decreases**, the melting temperature **increases**.
* As pressure **increases**, the melting temperature **decreases**.

At the triple point (≈ 611 Pa, 0.006 atm, 0.01 °C) water can coexist as solid, liquid, and vapor.  
Going from the triple‑point pressure up to 10 kPa (still well below 1 atm) moves along this melting line toward a slightly higher temperature. The shift is modest—only a few hundredths of a degree—because the slope is shallow over this pressure range.

---

### Quick reference

| Pressure | Boiling Point | Freezing (Melting) Point |
|----------|---------------|--------------------------|
| 1 atm (101.3 kPa) | 100 °C | 0 °C |
| 10 kPa | ≈ 45 °C | ≈ +0.01 °C |
| 0.1 kPa (triple point) | 0.01 °C | 0.01 °C |

> **Note:** These values assume pure, ideal water. Impurities, dissolved gases, or other substances will depress the freezing point further (freezing point depression).

---

### Bottom line

If you’re measuring or modeling water at 10 kPa, treat its freezing point as essentially **0 °C** (within a few hundredths of a degree). This is why, for most practical purposes, you can still say “water freezes at 0 °C” even when the pressure is reduced to 10 kPa.
